claims.text: Integrating high-throughput vibrational-property calculations with machine learning will identify low-phonon-thermal-conductivity HEAs more accurately than composition-only baselines.
The target materials are single-phase random solid-solution HEAs with maintained chemical disorder.
The proposed model couples first-principles phonon calculations with statistical learning to derive features related to phonon scattering.
The approach is applicable to HEAs with uniform random atomic distributions.
The approach is applicable when elemental mass and bonding variations are moderate enough to be represented by calculable vibrational features.
Phonon band structure and vibrational density of states mediate phonon scattering caused by mass and force-constant disorder.
Calculated phonon dispersion and local vibrational modes capture the effect of configurational disorder on phonon scattering.
Vibrational features improve the mapping between microstructural disorder and low thermal conductivity relative to average compositional descriptors.
The proposed approach will improve predictive accuracy by at least 30% over the baseline.
The proposed approach will successfully identify HEAs with experimentally verified reductions in phonon thermal conductivity.
Current baseline methods primarily use compositional correlations or averaged physical parameters without directly incorporating vibrational dynamics.
Extremely large disparities in atomic radius, mass, or bonding character can make phonon calculations unreliable.
Phase separation would cause the materials to deviate from the assumed single-phase disordered state and limit applicability.
Direct experimental evidence that first-principles phonon spectral features improve predictive accuracy in HEAs is limited.
Thermal-conductivity measurements by TDTR or laser-flash analysis can be used to benchmark the predictions.
Failure to obtain at least a 30% accuracy improvement over the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
The hypothesis would also be falsified if more than 70% of samples predicted to have low conductivity fail to meet the experimental low-conductivity threshold.
